title: Sura and Pumbedita
hookLine: the great academies of Babylonia become the center of learning

lines: WHERE DID THESE SCHOLARS COME FROM?
cards: Maybe you're from Pumbedita, where they pass an elephant through the eye of a needle. That's the Talmud's teasing reply to an argument a little too clever.
Pumbedita was a town in Babylonia, and apparently its scholars had a reputation: they could make anything fit through anything. It's a joke, with a compliment hiding inside.
To earn a name like that, a town needs a lot of people arguing about texts for a very long time. So where were they, and how did a school in Babylonia end up with that kind of name?

teach.b: Babylonia, the land between the rivers, had a Jewish community from the time of the exile.

Psalm 137 remembers it in grief, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "By the rivers of Babylon, There we sat down, yea, we wept, When we remembered Zion." Centuries later, that land of weeping became a place of learning.
Two towns stand out in the story: Sura and Pumbedita. Each had its academy, a yeshiva, with a head, students, and a way of reading the Mishnah all its own.
Tradition tells that Rav, a student who had learned in the land of Israel, came down to Babylonia and taught at Sura. The elephant joke suggests Pumbedita had a name for clever argument.
The Talmud also speaks of public gatherings for learning called the kallah, where crowds came to listen, and it has a line about that crowd: the reward for attending the kallah is the crowding.
You're packed in, elbow to elbow, and that is the point.
Learning moves. It doesn't belong to one city.
The conversation that began in the land of Israel went on by other rivers, as people carried the Mishnah in their memories and their scrolls, and opened new rooms to argue in.

how: Jewish study still often happens in a yeshiva or study hall, and some communities hold gatherings for adult learning inspired by the old kallah months of Babylonia.

games.q: you live in Babylonia. a kallah gathering is coming at the academy, and the hall will be packed. what do you do?
o: go, and stand in the crowd.
games.why: the Talmud says the reward of the kallah is the crowding. being packed in was part of the learning.

practice: Think of the places you actually learn: a kitchen table, a bus seat, a library, a friend who explains things well.
Pick one, see it clearly, and ask what would make it a better room for learning, a book left out, a regular time, another person to learn with; the academies were people as much as buildings.
If you pray, you can ask for a place and a partner to learn with.

wordCard.voice: Yeshiva. An academy for studying the Mishnah and Talmud, the kind that made the Babylonian towns of Sura and Pumbedita well-known for learning.

orig.note: Hebrew: yeshiva, an academy; the word is tied to sitting, sitting to learn.

carryVoice: Your line: learning moves. The conversation found new rivers to sit beside. Nine hundred nine days now.
